description: In love with learning, exploring, and teaching in ways that are creative and effective.
summary:
OUTBOUND is a browser game in which the player designs, flies and reviews a complete space science mission. Each expedition starts with a real science question, from mapping safe landing ground on the Moon to sounding Europa's ice. The player signs a funding partner, picks the question, chooses a launch vehicle, fits a spacecraft from 18 modules under budget and mass limits, and plots a course where every stop trades fuel, power, radiation and science. A flight readiness review then flies the exact plan through the game's own flight model and gives a GO / NO-GO forecast before launch.

The flight is played through five operations: instrument acquisition, debris avoidance, repair, solar pointing and data downlink. Only data that reaches Earth counts. Every flight ends with a NASA-style mission report that separates the proximate cause from root causes and names a corrective action.

Twelve expeditions across four chapters use real distances, so sunlight, link capacity, cruise time and launch energy follow physics. The game lets students experience how one design decision constrains every other part of a mission.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
OUTBOUND walks the player through a whole mission, from concept to post-flight review:
1. Partner: choose one sponsor. Each brings a grant and one free module.
2. Question: twelve science questions in four chapters (Moon; Mars and Vesta; Europa and Io; Enceladus, Titan and Triton). Each needs an image, thermal or radar instrument and has its own hazards.
3. Vessel: choose a launch vehicle (light, medium, heavy) and fit up to 18 modules. Budget and launch mass are hard limits, and a farther target leaves less payload.
4. Course: one stop per layer, three ways through each, for example a short debris lane, a radiation shortcut or a long clear arc that costs fuel, time and power.
5. Flight readiness review: the plan is flown through the real flight model at three skill levels and summarised as five margins, a readiness figure and a GO / NO-GO call.
6. Flight: travel in real time and operate five stations: instrument acquisition, debris avoidance, welding repair, solar array pointing and Earth downlink.
7. Mission report: success against baseline and threshold science, the launch / space / ground / user segments, a chain showing where each data packet was lost, a cause analysis and lessons learned.

HOW THE SCIENCE IS HANDLED
One measured input per destination, its distance from the Sun, drives the rest: sunlight (inverse square), signal delay, Hohmann cruise time and launch energy (C3). Solar recharge, link capacity and payload capacity follow from those. The science question selects the instrument: camera images never answer a thermal or radar question. Credits, mass units and damage values are game abstractions, and the game says so.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Students usually meet orbits, power or communications one at a time. Here a heavier instrument needs a bigger launch vehicle, a far target removes solar power, and data that is not downlinked is not science. Every module is rated for every expedition with a one-line reason, so the player sees why hardware matters in that place. The mission report teaches why a mission failed, not only that it failed.

CREATIVITY
The same five operations serve all twelve expeditions; the environment and the fitted hardware change how hard each one is. A scripted pilot model flies every plan through the real engine. It powers the in-game forecast and was also used to balance the campaign.

TOOLS
TypeScript, Next.js, React, HTML Canvas 2D, GSAP, Node.js test runner (185 rule tests), Playwright for browser checks, Vercel with Vercel Blob for hosting and saves.

FACTORS CONSIDERED
Accessibility for beginners (a companion guide, tooltips, a practice lab for each operation), honest labelling of what is real physics and what is game abstraction, saves per browser with several slots, and no account or personal data.

USE OF AI
AI coding assistants wrote and reviewed large parts of the code and tests under the team's direction. Background and equipment artwork was produced with AI image generation; prompts and lineage are recorded in docs/ART-PROVENANCE.json in the repository. Mission texts were drafted with AI assistance and checked against the NASA sources listed below.
